extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants/patent attorneys (practitioners involved in patent prosecution, Korean context)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing novelty/obviousness (inventive step) of patent claims across invention types (selection, numerical limits, parameters, product-by-process, combination inventions), including how advantageous effects, common practice, and secondary evidence affect the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common practice / ordinary creativity
rubrics_metrics.description: A technical feature that is commonly practiced without exercising any ingenuity is not considered inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making a penetrating hole in an outer surface to observe inner space is commonly practiced and not inventive; adopting a tray for ball grid array components that is prevalent at filing is not inventive as a skilled person would adopt it without special difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantageous effects considered to support inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: If an effect achieved by matters defining a claimed invention is advantageous in comparison with an effect of a prior art reference, it is taken into consideration as a fact to affirmatively support its inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an advantageous effect compared to the prior art is so remarkable that it could not have been foreseen by a person skilled in the art from the state of the art, inventive step may not be denied (Supreme Court decision examples). Conversely, inventions made by collecting/improving publicly known arts are not considered inventive except where: it is difficult to collate the arts and achieve a new advantageous effect beyond what was expected; or a new technical method is added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitatively different or quantitatively prominent effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claimed invention appears easily made by combining prior art references at first glance, an inventive step can be acknowledged if the claimed invention has an advantageous effect that is qualitatively different or quantitatively prominent compared with those of the prior art references, and the effect could not have been foreseen by a person skilled in the art from the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly important for selection inventions and chemical inventions where product effect is hard to predict from structure. Example: mixing chemical compounds in a certain ratio that yields unexpected results can support inventive step (Supreme Court decision cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence/arguments for effects not explicitly disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Though an advantageous effect may be superior to the prior art and not explicitly disclosed, the examiner can assess inventive step from applicant's arguments and evidence (e.g., experiment results) if the effect is easily recognized by a person skilled in the art from the description and structure shown in drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the asserted effect is not supported by the description/drawings and is not inferable therefrom, the effect from the argument should not be considered in assessing inventive step. Example: half-open barrel in a blood-cupping device—if effects are remarkably ensured from the description and common knowledge, inventive step may be considered; otherwise applicant must submit experimental comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection invention criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A selection invention selects a species from a genus disclosed in prior art (including selection of matter not directly disclosed in the prior art as an essential element). Selection by experimentation of an optimized means from publicly known technology is normally not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A selection invention can have inventive step if it achieves advantageous effect versus prior art. All specific means in the selection should have advantageous effects qualitatively different or quantitatively prominent. The description should precisely explain the advantageous effect; experimental materials are not required but may be submitted if the effect is doubted. Example: selection achieving ten times greater oral activity than prior art supports inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical limitation inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions with indispensible elements expressed by numerical values. Experimentally selecting an optimal numerical range from publicly known art is normally considered ordinary creativity and inventive step is generally denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claimed invention involves inventive step if it has a more advantageous effect within the limited numerical range than the prior art; the advantageous effect should be remarkably improved across the whole range. Criteria for 'critical significance' include: (1) required regarding any part of the numerical range if the invention is in line with prior art; (2) not required if two inventions solve different problems and have qualitatively different effects even if configurations differ only by numerical limitation. For recognition: (a) remarkable change in effect across the boundary, (b) technical meaning of limitation described in the specification, (c) embodiments or supplemental materials proving upper/lower limits are critical, and (d) objective confirmation generally via experimental results covering the whole range. Examples illustrate when a numerical limitation is technically meaningless or when improved quality/economy supports inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parameter invention criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A parameter invention creates a certain (nonstandard) parameter, parameterizes it mathematically using correlations among parameters, and employs it as part of essential claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine inventive step after defining the subject matter from the specification/drawings/common knowledge. Consider functions/characteristics caused by the parameter; do not compare claimed invention to prior art without accounting for functions/characteristics. If parameter is merely a different expression or confirmation of intrinsic features and the cause-effect link to advantageous effect is weak, inventive step is denied. If the parameter invention is effectively a numerical limitation, apply numerical-limitation criteria. Examiner may notify applicant of concrete grounds for rejection and propose solutions when reasonable doubt exists; if the parameter is standard/common, the special criteria do not apply. Examples and possible examiner actions (notify, describe grounds concretely, propose solutions) are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: product interpreted by properties/structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A product claim expressed by its manufacturing process must have the manufacturing process construed as a limitation defining the structure and properties of the final product; the subject matter sought is the final product, not the process or apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and inventive step are determined by comparing the product (with structure/properties defined by claim limitations) to publicly known products. If the manufacturing process affects product structure/properties, inventive step is determined for the product having those properties. If process affects only efficiency/yield and not product properties, inventive step is determined solely on the final product ignoring the process. Where structure/properties are hard to infer from the process, examiner shall define scope using the whole specification (including experimental data/embodiments/drawings) and may issue a rejection. If prior art discloses the same/similar manufacturing process, the examiner may infer same product and reject for lack of inventive step. Several examples (pharmaceutical extraction steps; belt coupling device; polarizing film) illustrate application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination invention: whole-claim assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination invention gathers technical features disclosed in prior art as a whole to solve a technical problem; the claim should be considered as a whole and inventive step should not be negated merely because each claim element is known from prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining inventive step, assess difficulty in forming structurally combined elements as a whole (problem-solution approach) and consider unique effects of the invention as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining multiple prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may determine inventive step by combining more than two prior art references (including well-known or commonly used art), but such combination is limited to cases where a person skilled in the art could easily combine the references at the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No strict limit on the number of references, but the examiner mainly considers whether prior art contains a motivation or suggestion to combine. Consider state of the art, common general knowledge, technical trends, and industry demands; if combination deemed easily made by a skilled person, inventive step may be denied. Examples: substituting an image sensor for an optical sensor or separating game program/data are shown as obvious combinations given the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation/suggestion standard for combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether a prior art disclosure contains a motivation, suggestion, or the like for a combination is made synthetically by assessing whether the motivation/suggestion is explicitly taught, inherent from the technical problem, or part of common general knowledge or empirical rules of a skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: change of material for a baby carriage transparent window may be obvious if a public report warned about flexible plastics and rigid plastic was known not to cause the problem and that fact was common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining well-known technology: exception when synergistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining a well-known technology with another prior art disclosure is normally considered obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if the combined technical feature (even if well-known) yields an advantageous effect as a result of the combination, the combination may not be regarded as obvious. Examiner should look for such advantageous or unexpected effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergistic effect vs aggregation (juxtaposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a combination invention achieves an effect by functional interaction between technical features that is different from or greater than the sum of individual effects (synergistic effect), inventive step may be recognized; if the claim is merely a juxtaposition or aggregation of known features without meaningful interaction, inventive step may be denied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether modification/substitution leads to structural difficulties or yields effects greater than the summed effects of prior art. Examples: combinations that merely substitute known parts without added functional advantage are treated as aggregation and are obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindsight and reliance on many references
rubrics_metrics.description: If forming the claimed invention requires reliance on a large number of prior art references or combining references only with hindsight, this may indicate improper hindsight and weaken the examiner's rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging whether it would have been obvious to combine references, examiner should consider: (i) whether a skilled person would have good reason to combine them, (ii) whether the prior arts are from similar or neighboring technical fields, and (iii) whether there is a reasonable basis to associate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis principle and other factors in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: In principle, determination of inventive step synthesizes the objective, technical configuration, and functional effect of the claimed invention; but other factors may also be taken into account and the examiner should not readily deny inventive step without considering applicant arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other factors include: (i) prior art teaching away the claimed invention may prevent denying inventive step (but mere description of prior art as inferior does not necessarily teach away), (ii) commercial success, favorable industry comments, or long-unimplemented demand may be secondary evidence indicative of inventive step but alone are insufficient and must be tied to technical features disclosed in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations (commercial success etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success, favorable comments from industry, or the fact that the invention had not been implemented for a long time before filing may be regarded as indicative of inventive step as secondary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such facts alone are not sufficient. Inventive step should be determined based on the specification's contents (objective, configuration, effect). Commercial success is not a criterion if it derives from non-technical factors (e.g., sales techniques, advertising). Example given where huge sales alone do not prove inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when reasonable doubt exists (parameter inventions and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiner has reasonable doubt (e.g., for parameter inventions) that the claimed invention is easily derived from prior art, the examiner can notify the applicant of grounds for rejection without strict comparison and should concretely describe the grounds and, if necessary, propose a solution to overcome rejection grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant refutes the grounds successfully the examiner cancels them; if not overcome, the examiner may decide rejection under Article 29(2). The examiner should detail the reasonable doubts (e.g., conversion of parameters by different definitions/measurement methods leading to similarity).
